# The problem this package solves

Landscape ecology separates **composition** (how much of what is present) from
**configuration** (how it is arranged in space). That distinction is the
backbone of patch-based analysis. When landscapes are represented as continuous
surfaces instead of patch mosaics, the distinction was never carried across.

Most of the metrics used on continuous surfaces are functions of the *multiset*
of values in the analysis neighbourhood: the amplitude family of surface
metrics (`Sa`, `Sq`, `Ssk`, `Sku`, `S10z`), the surface-bearing family derived
from the Abbott curve (`Sbi`, `Sci`, `Svi`, `Sk`, `Spk`, `Svk`), and the
information-theoretic measures (Shannon entropy, Rao's quadratic entropy).
Rearranging every pixel inside the neighbourhood leaves them numerically
unchanged. They cannot detect a change in spatial structure, in any landscape,
at any scale.

`surfscape` provides two things: a test that establishes this for any metric,
and a decomposition that separates the part of an observed change that is due
to the value distribution from the part that is due to spatial arrangement.

```{r load}
library(terra)
library(surfscape)

z1 <- rast(system.file("extdata", "ndvi_2013.tif", package = "surfscape"))
z2 <- rast(system.file("extdata", "ndvi_2023.tif", package = "surfscape"))
c(mean_2013 = global(z1, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1],
  mean_2023 = global(z2, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1])
```

```{r plot-data, fig.height = 2.8}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 3))
plot(z1, axes = FALSE, main = "NDVI 2013")
plot(z2, axes = FALSE, main = "NDVI 2023")
plot(z2 - z1, axes = FALSE, main = "difference",
     col = hcl.colors(100, "Blue-Red 3"))
```

# Which metrics can see arrangement?

`ss_sensitivity()` samples neighbourhoods, permutes the values inside each one,
and compares the observed metric with its permuted values. The permutation
preserves the value multiset exactly, so a metric that depends only on that
multiset is invariant.

```{r sens}
s <- ss_sensitivity(z1, w = 15, n = 400, nperm = 49, seed = 1)
s[, c("metric", "family", "arrangement", "csi", "effect")]
```

Two columns answer two different questions. `arrangement` states whether a
metric *can* respond to configuration as a matter of construction. `csi`, the
configurational sensitivity index, states how much it *does* respond in this
particular landscape: it is `1 - R^2` of the observed metric regressed on its
permutation mean, so zero means arrangement contributes nothing.

Metrics from other packages can be audited on exactly the same footing with
`ss_sensitivity_fun()`, which takes any function of a neighbourhood matrix.

```{r sens-fun}
f <- function(m) {
  v <- as.numeric(m)
  d <- v - mean(v)
  c(sd            = sqrt(mean(d^2)),
    skewness      = mean(d^3) / mean(d^2)^1.5,
    shannon       = {p <- table(cut(v, 16)) / length(v); p <- p[p > 0]
                     -sum(p * log(p))},
    mean_sq_diff  = mean((m[, -ncol(m)] - m[, -1])^2))
}
ss_sensitivity_fun(z1, f, w = 15, n = 120, nperm = 19, seed = 1)
```

The first three are invariant to machine precision; only the last responds to
how the values are arranged.

# Decomposing change

`ss_decompose()` splits the change in a metric between two dates into three
additive components:

* **global** -- the landscape-wide value distribution shifted;
* **local** -- values were redistributed among neighbourhoods;
* **config** -- values were rearranged *within* neighbourhoods.

The three sum exactly to the total change. The global component uses a rank
transfer between the two dates (`ss_rank_transfer()`), which keeps one date's
spatial arrangement and gives it the other date's value distribution; the split
is symmetrised over both orderings so that it does not depend on which date is
taken first.

```{r decomp}
d <- ss_decompose(z1, z2, metrics = c("sq", "sent", "sr1", "gcon"), w = 15)
names(d)
```

Additivity is exact, not approximate:

```{r additivity}
v <- values(d[[c("sr1_total", "sr1_global", "sr1_local", "sr1_config")]])
max(abs(v[, 1] - rowSums(v[, 2:4])), na.rm = TRUE)
```

For an aspatial metric the configuration component is exactly zero everywhere,
which is the point:

```{r zero-config}
range(values(d[["sq_config"]]), na.rm = TRUE)
range(values(d[["sent_config"]]), na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r decomp-plot, fig.height = 2.8}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 3))
for (k in c("sr1_total", "sr1_local", "sr1_config")) {
  r <- d[[k]]
  mx <- max(abs(quantile(values(r), c(.02, .98), na.rm = TRUE)))
  plot(clamp(r, -mx, mx, values = TRUE), axes = FALSE, main = k,
       range = c(-mx, mx), col = hcl.colors(100, "Blue-Red 3"))
}
```

# How the components scale

Composition and configuration do not respond to window size in the same way, so
the scale of analysis changes not only the magnitude of a result but which
process it is attributed to.

```{r scale}
sp <- ss_scale_profile(z1, z2, metrics = c("sq", "sr1"),
                       w_seq = c(5, 11, 21, 31))
sp
```

# Field sites

`ss_extract()` summarises the decomposed change in circular buffers around
point locations at several radii, returning a tidy long table ready for
multi-scale modelling.

```{r extract}
set.seed(1)
pts <- data.frame(
  id = 1:6,
  x  = runif(6, xmin(z1) + 600, xmax(z1) - 600),
  y  = runif(6, ymin(z1) + 600, ymax(z1) - 600))
e <- ss_extract(d, pts, radii = c(150, 300, 600))
head(e, 10)
```

# Practical notes

* Always pass the same `range` to both dates when metrics involve binning
  (`sent`, `srao`, and the GLCM family). `ss_decompose()` does this for you.
* `csi` is landscape-specific; `arrangement` is not. A metric with
  `arrangement = TRUE` but a low `csi` is formally able to see configuration but
  carries little configurational information in the data at hand.
* The decomposition is an algebraic identity, so it is exact for any metric,
  including metrics supplied by other packages through the rank-transfer route.
* Large rasters are processed block-wise; results are identical to an in-memory
  pass.
